summary.title: Web3 Token Bridge (Ethereum <-> Arbitrum)
summary.description: Threat model for a cross-chain token bridge: users lock ERC-20 tokens in an Ethereum bridge contract, a relayer/validator server attests the lock and relays a signed message to an Arbitrum bridge contract that mints the wrapped token. Modeled with the experience-based WEB3 methodology.

text.text:
Token Bridge: Ethereum <-> Relayer Server <-> Arbitrum
WEB3 methodology (experience-based)

threats.title: Wallet connection / session hijack
threats.description: The dApp<->wallet connection (injected provider, WalletConnect, deep link) can be hijacked or spoofed: a malicious page reuses an approved session, a rogue relay MITMs the WalletConnect bridge, or a look-alike origin is granted account access. The user may then be prompted to sign attacker-controlled requests believing they come from the legitimate app.
threats.mitigation: Pin and display the connected origin; verify chainId before every request; scope and expire WalletConnect sessions and show active sessions to the user; re-authenticate with a fresh nonce (EIP-4361 Sign-In-With-Ethereum) rather than trusting a persisted connection; never auto-approve eth_requestAccounts. Ref: SCSVS-WALLET, EIP-4361.

threats.title: Blind signing of malicious payloads
threats.description: The user signs a transaction or an off-chain message (eth_signTypedData / personal_sign / permit) whose true effect is opaque in the wallet UI. Attackers exploit this with unlimited token approvals, Permit/Permit2 signatures, setApprovalForAll, or Seaport/'0x' order signatures that drain assets without an on-chain transaction from the victim.
threats.mitigation: Present human-readable transaction simulation and decoded calldata before signing (EIP-712 structured data, wallet 'what will happen' preview); warn on approvals to unknown spenders and on infinite allowances; scope approvals to exact amounts and expire them; use Permit2 allowance expiries; educate users to reject blind hex signatures. Ref: EIP-712, SWC-onchain-approval patterns, SCSVS.

threats.title: Reentrancy
threats.description: An external call (ETH transfer, ERC-777/ERC-721 hook, or arbitrary callee) is made before state is finalized, letting the callee re-enter the function or a sibling function and act on stale state - classic single-function, cross-function, and read-only reentrancy (SWC-107). This is architecturally represented here as a checklist prompt on the contract element; it is NOT auto-detected.
threats.mitigation: Apply checks-effects-interactions: update all state before external calls. Add a nonReentrant guard (OpenZeppelin ReentrancyGuard) on state-changing entry points; beware read-only reentrancy in view functions used by other protocols; treat token-transfer callbacks (ERC-777/1155/721) as reentrancy vectors. DETECT with Slither (reentrancy-* detectors), Mythril, and Foundry invariant/fuzz tests - this tool only flags the risk to review. Ref: SWC-107, SCSVS-CODE.

threats.title: Broken / missing access control
threats.description: Privileged functions (mint, withdraw, upgrade, setOwner, pause, parameter setters) lack correct authorization, use tx.origin for auth (SWC-115), leave an initializer callable by anyone (uninitialized proxy/owner), or have default/unprotected visibility (SWC-100/SWC-105). Attackers seize ownership or drain funds.
threats.mitigation: Gate every privileged function with explicit role checks (OpenZeppelin Ownable/AccessControl); never authorize with tx.origin - use msg.sender; ensure initializers run exactly once and are access-controlled; make sensitive functions explicitly external/internal with the right modifiers; use a timelock + multisig for admin actions. DETECT with Slither (suicidal, arbitrary-send, tx-origin) and manual review. Ref: SWC-100, SWC-105, SWC-115, SCSVS-AUTH.

threats.title: Proxy / upgradeability flaws
threats.description: Upgradeable-contract pitfalls: storage-layout collision between proxy and implementation or across upgrades, unprotected upgrade function, uninitialized implementation, delegatecall to attacker-controlled code (SWC-112), or a self-destructible/replaceable logic contract. A bad upgrade can rewrite all state or brick the system. Applies when this contract is marked upgradeable.
threats.mitigation: Use a vetted proxy pattern (OpenZeppelin UUPS/Transparent) and its storage-gap and initializer conventions; never change storage layout incompatibly; protect and timelock the upgrade path behind multisig; initialize implementations; forbid delegatecall to untrusted targets. DETECT with slither-check-upgradeability / OpenZeppelin Upgrades plugin. Ref: SWC-112, SCSVS-ARCH.

threats.title: Cross-chain bridge / relayer trust
threats.description: Bridging relies on off-chain validators, multisigs, or message relayers to attest events on another chain. A compromised validator set, forged proof, replayed message, or paused-but-unwound state can mint unbacked assets or lock user funds. Bridges are among the highest-value web3 targets historically.
threats.mitigation: Prefer light-client / proof-based verification over trusted-multisig bridges; enforce per-message replay protection (unique nonces, consumed-message registry) and per-epoch mint caps/rate limits; require strong, decentralized validator thresholds with timelocked upgrades; monitor mint/burn invariants and add circuit breakers. Ref: SCSVS-CROSSCHAIN.

threats.title: Unchecked / unsafe external call return
threats.description: The return value of a low-level call/send/delegatecall or a non-reverting ERC-20 transfer is not checked (SWC-104), so a failed transfer or callee revert is silently ignored and the contract continues in an inconsistent state - e.g. crediting a withdrawal that never paid out, or trusting a token that returns false instead of reverting.
threats.mitigation: Check the boolean success of every low-level call and revert on failure; use SafeERC20 (safeTransfer/safeTransferFrom) for tokens that don't revert; prefer pull-payments; handle both revert and false-return token behaviors. DETECT with Slither (unchecked-lowlevel, unchecked-transfer). Ref: SWC-104, SCSVS-CODE.

threats.title: Gas griefing / unbounded external work
threats.description: A function forwards user-controlled gas to an external call, loops over caller-supplied arrays, or does unbounded work, letting an attacker force out-of-gas, waste relayer gas (meta-tx), or make a subcall silently fail while the outer call succeeds (SWC-126 insufficient gas griefing).
threats.mitigation: Bound loop lengths and per-call work; check the success flag of low-level calls; avoid forwarding all remaining gas to untrusted callees; use pull-payment patterns; for meta-transactions verify the relayer cannot grief the signer. Ref: SWC-126, SWC-113.

threats.title: Private key / seed phrase exposure
threats.description: Private keys or seed phrases are stored, transmitted, or backed up insecurely: plaintext in localStorage/files/env vars, unencrypted cloud backups, keys held in application memory longer than needed, or a single hot key controlling high-value operations. Compromise leads to irreversible loss of all controlled assets.
threats.mitigation: Never store raw keys in browser storage, source, or logs. Use OS keystore / hardware wallet / secure enclave; encrypt at rest with a strong KDF; prefer signing in a hardware or MPC/threshold signer so the raw key is never assembled. Separate hot (low-value, rotatable) from cold (high-value) keys; consider a multisig (e.g. Safe) for treasury. Ref: SCSVS-KEY, NIST key management.

threats.title: Signature / cross-chain replay
threats.description: A signed message or transaction lacks binding to a unique context and can be replayed: reused on another chain (missing chainId / EIP-155), replayed after a fork, or a meta-transaction/permit reused because the nonce or domain separator is missing or reusable (SWC-121 missing protection against signature replay).
threats.mitigation: Bind every signature to chainId, a contract-specific EIP-712 domain separator, and a per-signer nonce that is consumed on use; include deadlines; invalidate signatures on upgrade; follow EIP-155 for raw transactions. Ref: SWC-121, SWC-117, EIP-712, EIP-155.

threats.title: Integer overflow / underflow / precision loss
threats.description: Arithmetic wraps or truncates: overflow/underflow in unchecked blocks or pre-0.8 Solidity (SWC-101), rounding/precision loss in fixed-point math, division-before-multiplication, or unsafe casts that silently truncate. Leads to mis-accounting, free mints, or drained balances.
threats.mitigation: Use Solidity >=0.8 checked arithmetic and justify every 'unchecked' block; use audited fixed-point libraries (e.g. PRBMath, FullMath) and multiply-before-divide; validate and bound casts; add invariant/property fuzz tests (Foundry, Echidna) on conservation of value. DETECT with Slither and fuzzing. Ref: SWC-101, SCSVS-CODE.

threats.title: Malicious or MITM'd RPC endpoint
threats.description: The application trusts a single RPC/node endpoint for chain state and broadcast. A compromised, malicious, or MITM'd RPC can lie about balances, allowances, gas, and confirmations, censor or reorder transactions, or leak the user's IP/address graph for deanonymization.
threats.mitigation: Use HTTPS/WSS endpoints only; verify results against multiple independent providers for high-value reads; confirm receipts by block/log inclusion rather than trusting eth_call alone; allow users to configure a trusted RPC; consider light-client / proof verification where available. Do not embed a single hard-coded key-bearing RPC. Ref: SCSVS-COMMS.
